newsitem.title: USA: Race re-emerges in Simpson civil case.
newsitem.headline: Race re-emerges in Simpson civil case.

text.p: The racial issues that surrounded O.J. Simpson's criminal trial re-emerged during jury selection in his civil trial on Friday when a black man told how his white supervisors reacted to last year's not guilty verdicts.
"The supervisors were mad at me because O.J. won the case," the man, who appeared to be in his 30s, told the lawyers and judge in the civil trial.
When asked why, he said, "Maybe because I'm black."

Simpson, a black former football hero turned TV sports commentator and actor, was found not guilty last Oct. 3 of the June 12, 1994, stabbing murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman, both of whom were white.
He is currently fighting a wrongful deaths civil lawsuit brought by the families of the victims who are seeking financial damages to compensate them for the loss of their loved ones.
The black prospective juror, who works for a truck rental company, said his white supervisors, who had previously been friendly toward him, gave him the "brush-off" after the verdicts were announced.
"I felt like I was O.J. at the time," he added. Asked if he had taken any action against his supervisors he said, "I just let it go."

A lighter note was injected into the proceedings when a white prospective juror said he wrote in his questionnaire that Kato Kaelin, a witness in the criminal trial, appeared to be a "deadbeat who lived in O.J.'s guesthouse. Looks like a druggie."

The man, who appeared to be in his 50s, provoked further courtroom laughter when he said he may have been unfair to Kaelin, Simpson's houseguest who testified about Simpson's movements on the night of the murders. "He may be very good at what he does, but I don't know what he does."
Kaelin was a would-be actor before the trial but after his new-found celebrity he became a talk-show host, though his new career soon fizzled.

The man was one of five new prospective jurors, three blacks, two whites and an Asian, who were added to the panel that will go through a second round of questioning, starting sometime next week. By lunchtime Friday, 85 jurors were in that pool, which Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki has said he wants to bring up to 100 potential jurors.
